content.title: About
content.content: Barbecue pork, no sauce is pork meat cooked on a grill or smoker using a dry rub and marinade without any added sauces. The result is a smoky‑flavored, tender piece of meat with a slightly charred crust.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Barbecue pork is a staple of Southern US cuisine, often prepared over open fire.
Dry rubs typically contain paprika, garlic, onion, coriander, and black pepper.
Without sauce the meat retains the natural flavor of pork and is lower in calories than sauced versions.
Low‑temperature smoking (80‑120 °C) keeps the meat juicy while imparting a deep smoke aroma.
Wood types such as hickory or apple add distinct flavor notes to the pork.

items.title: High in protein
items.content: Pork provides complete protein essential for muscle growth and tissue repair.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Contains thiamine, niacin, and vitamin B12 which support energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Source of zinc and iron
items.content: These minerals are important for immune function, DNA synthesis, and oxygen transport.

items.title: Low in carbohydrates
items.content: Makes it suitable for low‑carb and keto diets.

items.title: Contains creatine
items.content: Creatine can help improve strength and endurance during physical activity.

items.title: High saturated fat content
items.content: Consuming large amounts of fatty pork may raise cholesterol levels.

items.title: Risk of overeating
items.content: Barbecue portions are often generous, leading to excess calorie intake.

items.title: Needs thorough cooking
items.content: Undercooked pork can harbor harmful bacteria such as Salmonella and Trichinella.

items.title: Spice allergies
items.content: Some individuals may be allergic to ingredients in the dry rub (e.g., mustard or pepper).

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Slice the cooked pork into thin strips or cubes and serve as a main dish, in salads, sandwiches, or as a snack. Pair with fresh vegetables, herbs, or a light yogurt‑based dip for balance.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep cooked pork in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3‑4 days. For longer storage, freeze in a vacuum‑sealed bag for 2‑3 months. Reheat to an internal temperature of at least 74 °C before eating.
